deed: Rainer Weiss, a Jewish refugee from Berlin, designed LIGO and discovered gravitational waves
title: Rainer Weiss fled the Nazis as a child, conceived LIGO, and the detector picked up gravitational waves for the first time

trailer.text: Rainer Weiss, a physicist and winner of the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics, was born in Berlin in 1932 to a Jewish father.
The family fled the Nazis, and in January 1939 it landed in New York.
While teaching a course at MIT, he conceived a class exercise, and the exercise became the idea for LIGO: an instrument designed to pick up ripples in space-time, known as gravitational waves.
On September 14, 2015, the two LIGO detectors picked up a gravitational-wave signal, and this was their first direct detection.
In 2017 Weiss shared the Nobel Prize for this work.

glance.value: Jewish father; the family fled the Nazis

stations.title: A child in Berlin, a family in flight

paragraphs.text: Rainer Weiss was born in Berlin in 1932.
His father was a doctor and psychoanalyst, and his mother was an actress.
According to JTA, his mother was not Jewish and his father was Jewish.
Weiss said that his father came from a well-off German Jewish family in Berlin that had connections to the Rathenau family.
According to The New York Times, the Nazis abducted the father shortly before his son was born.
Weiss said that his father had difficulties with Nazis who had infiltrated the hospital where he worked.
The family fled Nazi Germany to Prague.
Weiss said that a critical moment came in September 1938, when Chamberlain gave the Sudetenland to Hitler and effectively opened Czechoslovakia to the Nazis.
He also said that the Stix family of St Louis gave financial bond for about ten thousand Jewish professionals so that they could enter the United States.
In January 1939 the family landed in New York.
According to him, it took his father about four years to pass the New York State examinations and be certified as a medical doctor.
Weiss said that as a teenager he earned a little money by fixing radios and other electronic devices.
In 1950 he was accepted to MIT as a freshman.
In the spring of 1953 he became an electronics technician in the Atomic Beam Laboratory of Prof. Jerrold Zacharias at MIT.
According to him, the cesium clock developed in the laboratory was commercialized and became the time standard of the Bureau of Standards.
Weiss said that he wanted to work at Princeton with Prof. Robert Dicke, who was interested in gravitation.
According to him, the two years at Princeton were very important to his scientific development.
He then returned to MIT as a faculty member in the Physics department.
He said that his wife, Rebecca, was a plant physiologist at Harvard.
According to the MIT Department of Physics, Weiss returned to MIT as an assistant professor in 1964.

stations.title: A class exercise that became a detector

paragraphs.text: Weiss recounted that in 1966 he was asked to teach an advanced course in general relativity.
According to The New York Times, while teaching the course in the late 1960s, Weiss, a German-born American, sketched out the idea that became the LIGO project.
According to MIT News, the idea began as a class exercise.
Weiss said in 2017 that the idea came from the question of what the simplest thing was that would show students the influence of a gravitational wave.
Gravitational waves are like ripples in space-time, and they occur when objects with mass accelerate.
According to The New York Times, Weiss knew that the waves should stretch and squeeze space as they traveled through it, and envisioned a device that would measure those disruptions.
The detector uses lasers to measure small changes in length caused by gravitational waves.
Weiss said that the thought experiment from the course became, in 1972, a real experiment to detect gravitational waves from astronomical sources.
According to The New York Times, that year Weiss secured funding from MIT to build a small prototype.

stations.title: Balloons in the sky: the background radiation

paragraphs.text: Weiss said that between 1967 and 1982 he and his team flew around 20 high-altitude balloon flights, first to measure the spectrum of the cosmic background radiation and then its isotropy.
According to The New York Times, in the balloon experiments Weiss and Dirk Muehlner established the temperature of the background radiation to be 2.73 kelvin above absolute zero.
Weiss was chairman of the COBE science working group.
Two COBE scientists, Mather and Smoot, won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2006.
According to him, by the mid-1980s he was more involved in the gravitational wave project, and Stephan Meyer took over the background radiation research.
According to MIT News, in 1976 Weiss began working with Kip Thorne, and the two created a collaboration between MIT and Caltech.
According to The New York Times, Thorne, a theorist, was at first skeptical, and later became an enthusiastic supporter of the project.
In 1979 Ronald Drever of the University of Glasgow joined the effort at Caltech.
According to Physics World, in 1979 the National Science Foundation funded Caltech and MIT to develop the proposal to build LIGO.
The detectors were built in Hanford, Washington, and in Livingston, Louisiana.
LIGO is two identical detectors located 1,865 miles apart.
According to Physics World, the LIGO facilities opened in 2002.
According to The New York Times, the National Science Foundation invested more than a billion dollars in developing LIGO.
According to LIGO, Whitcomb said that Weiss was the first person to envision a large detector, and that he identified almost all of the problems that would need to be overcome.
According to The New York Times, about 1,500 scientists from about 100 institutions in 18 countries work on the LIGO and Virgo projects.
On September 14, 2015, the two LIGO detectors simultaneously picked up a transient gravitational-wave signal.
According to the discovery paper, this was the first direct detection of gravitational waves, and also the first observation of a binary black hole merger.
The signal-to-noise ratio was 24, and the false alarm rate was less than one event per 203,000 years.
The source lies at a luminosity distance of about 410 megaparsecs.
According to Space.com, the signal was designated GW150914.
According to Space.com, Einstein had been convinced that these ripples were too faint for any apparatus on Earth to detect.

stations.title: The Nobel Prize, and what remains after him

paragraphs.text: In 2017 Weiss shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.
The prize citation was for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.
According to JTA, Weiss won half of the $1.1 million prize, and Barish and Thorne shared the other half.
JTA wrote that three American scientists won the prize, and that one of them fled the Nazis with his parents.
According to The New York Times, a member of the Nobel committee said at the announcement that we now witness the dawn of a new field, gravitational wave astronomy.

In 2016 Weiss, together with Drever and Thorne, received the Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics, the Gruber Prize in Cosmology, the Shaw Prize in Astronomy and the Kavli Prize in Astrophysics.
He also shared the Princess of Asturias Award for Technical and Scientific Research with Thorne, Barish and the LIGO Scientific Collaboration.
At a press conference at MIT, Weiss said that the discovery is the work of many, many people who played crucial roles.
With the money from the Nobel Prize he established the Barish-Weiss Fellowship, which supports student research in the MIT Department of Physics.
Weiss died on August 25, 2025, at the age of 92.
Prof. Peter Fisher said that Weiss created two fields: measurements of the cosmic background radiation and gravitational waves.
Kip Thorne said of him that he is the most influential person the field has seen, by a large margin.
Weiss said that at MIT he failed all his courses and had to leave as a student.
According to him, the atomic fountain clock did not work, and the first attempt was made in a vertical vacuum system about 3 meters high.
He also said that the experiment at Princeton was unsuccessful.
According to The New York Times, Joseph Weber claimed he had found a way to detect gravitational waves in aluminum cylinders, but no one could replicate his experiments.
According to the newspaper, Weiss's idea was sound, but the question of whether it could be carried out encountered a great deal of resistance.
According to Physics World, after almost a decade of operation no waves had been detected, so in 2011 the two observatories were upgraded and made ten times more sensitive than before.
According to The New York Times, some thought that Weiss should have shared the 2006 Nobel Prize for COBE.

claims.text: לפי JTA, שלושה מדענים אמריקאים זכו בנובל בפיזיקה, ואחד מהם ברח מהנאצים עם הוריו.
claims.quote: Three American scientists were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics, including one who fled the Nazis with his parents

claims.text: לפי הניו יורק טיימס, חבר ועדת נובל אמר עם ההכרזה שכעת עדים לשחר תחום חדש: אסטרונומיית גלי כבידה.
claims.quote: We now witness the dawn of a new field: gravitational wave astronomy

claims.text: לפי MIT News, ב-2016 קיבל וייס את פרס פורצי הדרך המיוחד בפיזיקה יסודית, פרס גרובר בקוסמולוגיה, פרס שאו באסטרונומיה ופרס קאבלי באסטרופיזיקה, כולם במשותף עם דרבר ות'ורן.
claims.quote: In 2016, Weiss received a Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics, the Gruber Prize in Cosmology, the Shaw Prize in Astronomy, and the Kavli Prize in Astrophysics, all shared with Drever and Thorne.

claims.text: לפי MIT News, וייס שיתף גם את פרס אסטוריאס לקידמה טכנית ומדעית עם ת'ורן, בריש ושיתוף הפעולה המדעי של LIGO.
claims.quote: He also shared the Princess of Asturias Award for Technical and Scientific Research with Thorne, Barry Barish of Caltech, and the LIGO Scientific Collaboration.

claims.text: לפי MIT News, וייס אמר במסיבת עיתונאים ב-MIT שהגילוי הוא עבודתם של אנשים רבים רבים שמילאו תפקידים מכריעים.
claims.quote: The discovery has been the work of a large number of people, many of whom played crucial roles

claims.text: לפי MIT News, בכסף מפרס נובל הקים וייס את מלגת בריש-וייס לתמיכה במחקר סטודנטים במחלקה לפיזיקה ב-MIT.
claims.quote: With the money he received from the Nobel Prize, Weiss established the Barish-Weiss Fellowship to support student research in the MIT Department of Physics.

claims.text: לפי MIT News, וייס נפטר ב-25 באוגוסט (2025) בגיל 92.
claims.quote: a renowned experimental physicist and Nobel laureate whose groundbreaking work confirmed a longstanding prediction about the nature of the universe, passed away on Aug. 25.

claims.text: לפי MIT News, פרופ' פיטר פישר אמר שוייס היה יוצר שני תחומים: מדידות קרינת הרקע הקוסמית וגלי כבידה.
claims.quote: Rai held a singular position in science: He was the creator of two fields

claims.text: לפי MIT News, קיפ ת'ורן אמר על וייס שהוא האדם המשפיע ביותר בהפרש גדול שהתחום ראה.
claims.quote: He really is, by a large margin, the most influential person this field has seen.

claims.text: וייס סיפר שנכשל בכל הקורסים שלו ב-MIT ונאלץ לעזוב כסטודנט.
claims.quote: The result was I failed all my courses at MIT and had to leave as a student.

claims.text: וייס סיפר ששעון המזרקה האטומי לא עבד; הניסיון הראשון נעשה במערכת ואקום אנכית בגובה כ-3 מטרים.
claims.quote: Unfortunately, the fountain clock did not work. The first attempt was made in a vertical vacuum system about 3 meters high.

claims.text: לפי הניו יורק טיימס, ג'וזף ובר טען שמצא דרך לגלות גלי כבידה בגלילי אלומיניום, אך איש לא הצליח לשחזר את הניסויים.
claims.quote: Years earlier, the physicist Joseph Weber said he had found a way to detect gravitational waves, measuring how they compressed and elongated along the lengths of large aluminum cylinders. But no one could replicate the experiments.

claims.text: לפי הניו יורק טיימס, אף שהרעיון היה נכון, היתכנותו נתקלה בהתנגדות רבה.
claims.quote: Though the project idea was sound, its feasibility encountered a great deal of resistance.

claims.text: לפי Physics World, לאחר כמעט עשור של פעילות לא התגלו גלים, ולכן ב-2011 שודרגו שני המצפים לרגישות גבוהה פי עשרה.
claims.quote: After almost a decade of operation, however, no waves had been detected so in 2011 the two observatories were upgraded to make them 10 times more sensitive than before.

claims.text: לפי הניו יורק טיימס, היו שסברו שוייס היה צריך לחלוק את פרס נובל של 2006 על COBE.
claims.quote: Some thought that Dr. Weiss should have shared in that prize.

claims.text: לפי Physics World, האינטרפרומטר גילה גלי כבידה משני חורים שחורים ממוזגים במרחק של כ-1.3 מיליארד שנות אור.
claims.quote: the interferometer detected gravitational waves from two merging black holes some 1.3 billion light-years from Earth

claims.text: לפי הניו יורק טיימס, הגילוי של 2015 נבע מהתנגשות ומיזוג של שני חורים שחורים לפני כ-1.3 מיליארד שנים.
claims.quote: created by the collision and merging of two black holes about 1.3 billion years ago
